summary: Gives an overview of the design space for reliable multicast of bulk data and describes how application constraints affect possible solutions. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: Sending one big file to many people at once is tricky when some pieces get lost. This lays out the choices and which fit which needs.

questions: how to reliably multicast bulk data
how do multicast congestion control mechanisms work
subtitle: A guide to the tradeoffs in designing protocols to send bulk data reliably to many receivers.

tldr.problem: Sending a large amount of data reliably to many receivers at once is much harder than sending to one receiver. No single protocol design works for all applications because different applications have conflicting requirements.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2887 maps out the design space, categorizing the constraints from applications (scalability, reliability, ordering, latency) and networks (feedback paths, router support), and then describes various mechanisms (ACK-based, NACK-based, FEC, replication) for achieving good throughput and congestion control.
tldr.outcome: The RFC provides guidance that reliable multicast protocols should be built from reusable mechanism blocks rather than as monolithic standards, allowing applications with different needs to select appropriate combinations.

today: RFC 2887 remains an Informational RFC published in August 2000. It has not been obsoleted and serves as a foundational reference for understanding reliable multicast design. While no single universal reliable multicast protocol has emerged for the Internet, various protocols (PGM, RMTP, LMS) implement subsets of the mechanisms described in this RFC for specific use cases and network environments.

sections.title: The Challenge of Reliable Multicast
sections.content:
Reliable multicast is the problem of sending data from one sender to many receivers, ensuring all receivers get all the data, despite potential packet losses. Unlike unicast (one to one), where TCP guarantees reliability, multicast has no standard reliable transport.

RFC 2887 explains why there is no single solution: different applications need different things. A video streaming application does not need every packet; a file transfer does. A stock price feed needs low delay; a bulk data download does not. Some applications need to know that every receiver got the data; others do not. Some networks allow feedback from receivers to the sender; others do not (like satellite broadcasts).

The RFC surveys the design space and shows how application and network constraints force a choice from a range of possible mechanisms. The main message is that the right approach is to build reliable multicast from reusable mechanism blocks rather than standardizing complete protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending a message to one person is easy: ask them if they got it and resend if they say no. Sending the same message to a thousand people is much harder. This document explains the choices and when each choice makes sense.

sections.title: Application Constraints
sections.content:
Different applications have different requirements. A protocol must answer questions like:

  • Does everyone need to get the data? A software distribution service might not care if a few receivers miss pieces; a bank does.
  • How many receivers? Small systems can use mechanisms that do not scale to large groups.
  • Totally reliable or best effort? A file transfer needs every byte; audio broadcasting can tolerate some loss.
  • Low delay? Video streaming needs fast delivery; bulk file transfer does not.
  • Ordered delivery? Some applications need data in the order sent; others do not.
  • Feedback channel? Most networks allow receivers to send messages back to the sender, but satellite broadcasts do not.
  • Single sender? The RFC assumes a single sender sending to many; multiple senders add complexity not addressed here.

These constraints dramatically narrow the solution space. For example, if you need to know that every receiver got an application data unit (an ADU, a logical chunk like a file), you must receive positive acknowledgments from every receiver—a constraint that hurts scalability.
sections.plainLanguage: Does it matter if a few people miss it? Do a thousand people need it, or just ten? Is it okay if some arrives late? Is it super urgent? These questions change what strategy makes sense.

sections.title: Mechanisms for Good Throughput
sections.content:
RFC 2887 describes several mechanisms for detecting and recovering from packet loss:

ACK-based approaches: Receivers send positive acknowledgments (ACKs). The sender knows a packet was delivered if it receives an ACK. For tiny groups, every receiver ACKing every packet works. For larger groups, tree-based aggregation helps: receivers send ACKs up a tree, parents aggregate, reducing implosion at the root. However, trees require careful formation and maintenance.

NACK-based approaches: Receivers send negative acknowledgments only when they detect a missing packet. This scales much better because the sender only needs one NACK from any receiver to know a packet is missing; many receivers missing the same packet send only one NACK, thanks to suppression mechanisms. Suppression can use random timers (as in SRM) or other techniques (as in PGM). NACK-based is stateless at the sender: it does not need to track each receiver.

Replication: Some applications (like a shared text editor or a game position stream) continuously resend data. A new value supersedes an old one before retransmission is needed. This is efficient for applications where data naturally repeats.

Forward Error Correction (FEC): Instead of retransmitting lost packets, encode the data so that any k of n packets can reconstruct the original. Proactive FEC always sends extra packets; reactive FEC sends extras based on feedback. Layered FEC spreads encoded packets across multiple multicast groups, letting receivers join/leave to control their reception rate, enabling congestion control without feedback.
sections.plainLanguage: To recover from lost packets, you have choices: ask receivers to say 'I got it' (but this drowns the sender in messages for large groups); ask them to say 'I missed it' (cleaner for big groups); resend the same data over and over; or send extra math to let people reconstruct what they missed without resending.

sections.title: Congestion Control Strategies
sections.content:
Congestion control ensures the sender adapts to network conditions. RFC 2887 outlines five approaches:

  • Sender-controlled, one group: The sender uses feedback from receivers to control its send rate, slowing down when congestion is detected. The challenge is determining the rate that suits all receivers, from fastest to slowest.
  • Sender-controlled, multiple groups: Data is striped across multiple multicast groups at different rates. Application-level relays sit between groups, buffering and forwarding at different rates. This allows different receivers to receive at different speeds, but requires managing the relay infrastructure.
  • Receiver-controlled: Receivers decide if the sender is sending too fast and drop out of the group if congestion occurs. The remaining receivers experience better throughput. The challenge is coordinating many receivers to leave and rejoin.
  • Receiver-controlled, layered: Receivers join or leave multiple multicast groups to control their reception rate, based on their observations of packet loss. This can work in theory but requires coordination behind bottleneck links.
  • Router-based: Routers assist by filtering traffic, applying conditional joins, or fair queuing. This requires routers to understand and support the protocol, which is difficult to deploy on the public Internet but feasible in intranets.

Open-loop delivery using FEC pairs well with receiver-based congestion control, since neither requires feedback from receivers.
sections.plainLanguage: When the network is congested, someone has to slow down. The sender can throttle itself if it hears from receivers. Receivers can back off by joining fewer groups. Or routers can help. Pick whichever fits your network and application.

sections.title: Security and Design Principles
sections.content:
Security does not greatly constrain the design space for basic reliable multicast. Source authentication and data integrity are straightforward (sign and timestamp the data). For encryption and key re-keying to a large group, tree and graph-based solutions exist but do not directly affect the data distribution protocol.

A critical security issue: receivers themselves are untrusted. If an intermediate receiver retransmits data (which some protocols allow), the protocol must assume this receiver might be compromised. The original sender should sign the data so that receivers can verify it came from the legitimate source, even if retransmitted by an untrusted intermediate.

Denial-of-service is easier in multicast than unicast because any receiver can join and send feedback that affects all other receivers. A single receiver requesting retransmission of every packet could bring a session to a standstill. Senders must have policy to limit feedback and evict misbehaving receivers.

The RFC concludes by emphasizing that reliable multicast protocols should be built from reusable building blocks (ACK mechanisms, NACK mechanisms, FEC, replication) rather than as monolithic standards. This allows protocol evolution and reuse as new application constraints emerge.
sections.plainLanguage: Sign important data so people know it is real. Expect that some receivers might be bad actors, and plan for that. One angry receiver could break the whole session if you are not careful. Build from pieces, not from one giant standard.

items.title: ACK-based
items.text: Sender gets clear feedback but implosion at sender for large groups. Tree aggregation helps but requires topology.

items.title: NACK-based
items.text: Stateless at sender, scalable with suppression. Sender does not need to track receivers. Works for very large groups.

items.title: FEC
items.text: Reduces repair traffic and handles uncorrelated loss. Requires grouping data into rounds, adding latency.

items.title: Layered FEC
items.text: Enables receiver-controlled rate adaptation across multiple groups. Powerful but requires receiver coordination.
